items.foco: Most common cause of hypokalemia: diuretics
items.title: Most common cause of hypokalemia
items.contentHtml:
Most common cause of hypokalemia

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) and thiazides are the most common cause of acquired hypokalemia, due to increased distal potassium excretion secondary to greater tubular flow and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
  • The key pathophysiological mechanism is aldosterone-mediated renal potassium loss, stimulated by volume depletion.
  • In the differential diagnosis, hypokalemia due to redistribution (alkalosis, insulin, beta-agonists) and gastrointestinal losses (diarrhea, vomiting) must be ruled out.
  • The response to discontinuation of the diuretic confirms the etiology; If it persists, investigate primary hyperaldosteronism.

items.title: Normal Potassium Range
items.contentHtml:
Normal range of potassium

  • The normal range of serum potassium is 3.5-5.5 mEq/L. Values ​​<3.5 mEq/L define hypokalemia; >5.5 mEq/L define hyperkalemia.
  • Hypokalemia is classified as mild (3.0-3.4 mEq/L), moderate (2.5-2.9 mEq/L) and severe (<2.5 mEq/L).
  • Hyperkalemia is classified as mild (5.5-6.0 mEq/L), moderate (6.1-6.9 mEq/L) and severe (>7.0 mEq/L).
  • Small variations outside the normal range can have serious cardiac electrical consequences; The correction must be careful and monitored.

items.foco: ECG in hyperkalemia: peaked T wave
items.title: ECG in hyperkalemia
items.contentHtml:
If Potassium exceeds 8.0-9.0 mEq/L, the QRS merges with the T wave forming a sinusoidal wave, which precedes asystole or ventricular fibrillation.
  • The absence of changes in the electrocardiogram does not rule out severe hyperkalemia; Treatment should be guided by serum level and clinical symptoms.

items.foco: ECG in hypokalemia: prominent U wave
items.title: ECG in hypokalemia
items.contentHtml:
ECG in hypokalemia

  • The classic electrocardiographic finding of hypokalemia is the prominent U wave (visible in precordial leads V2-V3), which can be confused with a biphasic T wave.
  • Other changes include depression of the ST segment, flattening or inversion of the T wave, and increased amplitude of the P wave.
  • Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) can cause ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, especially in patients with ischemic heart disease or digitalis use.
  • Potassium correction reverses electrocardiographic changes; The presence of prominent U wave indicates the need for continuous monitoring.

items.title: Acute hyperkalemia treatment
items.contentHtml:
Acute hyperkalemia treatment

  • The first line in hyperkalemia with electrocardiographic changes or potassium >6.5 mEq/L is the administration of 10% calcium gluconate, 10-20 mL intravenously in 2-5 minutes, which stabilizes the cardiac membrane by antagonizing the effect of potassium.
  • gluconate calciumdoes not reduce serum potassium; It only protects the heart. Measures to reduce potassium should be followed: insulin plus intravenous glucose (10 IU of regular insulin + 50 mL of 50% glucose), nebulized salbutamol and exchange resins (sodium polystyrene sulfonate).
  • In refractory cases or with renal failure, consider urgent hemodialysis.
  • Do not administer calcium gluconate if the patient is being treated with digitalis due to the risk of poisoning. digitalis.

items.foco: Correction of hypokalemia: do not exceed 10-20 mEq/hour
items.title: Correction of hypokalemia
items.contentHtml:
Correction of hypokalemia

  • The rate of intravenous potassium replacement should not exceed 10-20 mEq/hour in adults without continuous cardiac monitoring; in critical units it can be increased up to 40 mEq/hour with electrocardiographic control.
  • The maximum daily dose is usually 200-400 mEq, but it depends on the severity and renal function.
  • Prefer oral administration whenever possible (lower risk of overcorrection); Every 40 mEq of oral potassium chloride raises serum potassium by approximately 0.25-0.5 mEq/L.
  • In severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) or with arrhythmias, replacement should be intravenous and in an infusion pump, without exceeding 10-20 mEq/hour in the peripheral route to avoid phlebitis.

items.foco: Pseudohyperkalemia due to hemolysis or tourniquet
items.title: Pseudohyperkalemia
items.contentHtml:
Pseudohyperkalemia

  • Pseudohyperkalemia is a false increase in serum potassium due to cellular release during sample collection or processing.
  • Main causes: hemolysis (most common), prolonged tourniquet (>1 minute), intense arm exercise, repeated puncture, prolonged storage, and severe thrombocytosis (>500,000/µL) or leukocytosis (>100,000/µL).
  • If suspected, repeat the measurement with correct technique: avoid a tourniquet, use an appropriate gauge needle, fill the tube without anticoagulant or with lithium heparin, process in less than 30 minutes.
  • If the elevated potassium does not correlate with the clinical status or the electrocardiogram, consider pseudohyperkalemia before treating.

items.foco: Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis: classic association
items.title: Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis
items.contentHtml:
Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis

  • Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis are classically associated in disorders with acid loss (vomiting, gastric aspiration) or use of diuretics.
  • Pathophysiology: intracellular potassium depletion stimulates renal reabsorption of bicarbonate and hydrogen excretion (contraction of extracellular volume), perpetuating alkalosis.
  • Correction of hypokalemia with potassium chloride is essential to reverse metabolic alkalosis; Without potassium replacement, alkalosis persists.
  • In the differential diagnosis of metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, consider primary hyperaldosteronism, Bartter syndrome and Gitelman syndrome.

items.foco: Hyperkalemia in renal failure: main mechanism
items.title: Hyperkalemia in kidney failure
items.contentHtml:
Hyperkalemia in renal failure

  • The main mechanism of hyperkalemia in renal failure is the reduction in renal potassium excretion due to a decrease in the glomerular filtration rate and, above all, an impairment of the distal secretion of potassium by the principal cells of the collecting duct.
  • In advanced chronic kidney disease (glomerular filtration rate <15-20 mL/min/1.73 m²), colonic adaptation (fecal excretion of potassium) becomes insufficient.
  • Aggravating factors: metabolic acidosis (displaces potassium to the extracellular space), drugs (inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, spironolactone, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and hyperglycemia.
  • Hyperkalemia in renal failure is a frequent indication of urgent hemodialysis if not responding to medical treatment.

items.title: Drug that causes hyperkalemia
items.contentHtml:
Drug that causes hyperkalemia

  • Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic aldosterone antagonist that blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct, reducing potassium secretion and causing hyperkalemia.
  • The risk increases with high doses (>25-50 mg/day), renal failure (filtration rate glomerular <30 mL/min/1.73 m²), concomitant use of inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and in the elderly.
  • Other drugs that cause hyperkalemia: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, amiloride, triamterene, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, heparin and non-selective beta-blockers.
  • Monitor serum potassium and renal function when starting spironolactone; if potassium >5.5 mEq/L, reduce dose or discontinue.

items.foco: Potassium in hypokalemic periodic paralysis: low
items.title: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
items.contentHtml:
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis

  • In hypokalemic periodic paralysis, serum potassium during the attack is low (<3.5 mEq/L), typically between 2.0-3.0 mEq/L, due to a massive shift of potassium from the extracellular to the intracellular space through defective calcium or sodium channels.
  • It is an autosomal channelopathy. dominant (mutation in CACNA1S or SCN4A) that affects skeletal muscle, producing symmetrical flaccid paralysis of the extremities, sparing respiratory and facial muscles.
  • Triggers include carbohydrates, rest after exercise, cold and stress; Potassium correction (oral or intravenous) reverses the paralysis.
  • Differential diagnosis: hypokalemic periodic paralysis thyrotoxic (more common in Asian men, with hyperthyroidism) and other causes of acute hypokalemia.

items.foco: Lethal rhythm in hyperkalemia: ventricular fibrillation
items.title: Lethal rhythm in hyperkalemia
items.contentHtml:
Lethal rhythm in hyperkalemia

  • The most feared lethal rhythm in hyperkalemia is ventricular fibrillation, which can degenerate into asystole if not treated immediately.
  • Previously, electrocardiographic progression includes peaked T wave, QRS widening, sine wave and cardiac arrest in fibrillation ventricular or asystole.
  • Ventricular fibrillation due to hyperkalemia requires immediate electrical defibrillation and simultaneous administration of intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize the membrane.
  • Prevention of lethal rhythm is based on early recognition of hyperkalemia and aggressive correction of serum potassium before arrhythmias appear ventricular.
